docs.title: CuTile Python From First Principles — Under Development
docs.text:
Writing Portable, Tile-Based GPU Kernels in NVIDIA cuTile Python, One Layer at a Time

This book is just getting started

This is the fifth sibling project to Mojo From First Principles, Triton From First Principles, CUDA From First Principles, and Rust From First Principles, built the same way: one chapter at a time, in page order, each one carrying real code and honestly labeled output. This book follows the Triton edition's arc rather than the CUDA/Mojo/Rust one: cuTile Python, like Triton, is a kernel-level DSL that leans on NumPy, CuPy, or PyTorch for the array itself and on PyTorch's autograd for the graph — it has no tensor type or autodiff engine of its own, and neither does this book build one. What this book owns is the tile kernel: the @ct.kernel functions, the tile/array type distinction, and the ahead-of-time compilation pipeline that is cuTile Python's actual point of difference from Triton. This book's verification story has its own two-tier split: every kernel definition and every ahead-of-time compilation to a named target architecture is genuinely run against the real cuda-tile package in this book's build environment — real cubin and Tile IR bytecode, byte-counted and shown. That environment has no NVIDIA GPU and no driver, so anything that requires an actual ct.launch() call against a live CUDA stream is explicitly tagged UNVERIFIED — pending real-GPU test rather than attempted and guessed at, until independently confirmed on real hardware and folded back in. Every chapter says plainly which of its claims rest on which kind of evidence.

"A kernel written against CUDA C++'s SIMT model answers the question 'what does thread (threadIdx.x, threadIdx.y, threadIdx.z) do?' A kernel written in cuTile Python never asks that question at all — it answers a different one: 'what does block pid do to the tile it just loaded?' The thread grid CUDA C++ makes you reason about explicitly is still there underneath, generated by the compiler instead of typed by hand. This book is about learning to think at that higher level honestly — without pretending the lower one has vanished."

This is a practitioner's guide to cuTile Python that follows the same arc as its Triton sibling rather than its CUDA C++, Mojo, or Rust ones: instead of building a tensor type and an automatic-differentiation engine from scratch, it treats cuTile Python the way it is actually positioned — a Python DSL for writing GPU kernels, plugged into PyTorch's existing tensor and autograd.Function machinery through custom forward/backward kernels, the same seam the Triton book uses. Where it necessarily departs from Triton is where cuTile Python itself is different: tiles and arrays are two distinct, statically-known types rather than one pointer-and-stride abstraction (an Array is mutable, strided, lives in global memory, and supports mostly load/store; a Tile is immutable, has a compile-time power-of-two shape, and supports the arithmetic, matmul, reduce, and scan operations a kernel actually computes with); and kernels are compiled ahead-of-time against a named target GPU architecture (ct.compilation.export_kernel(..., gpu_code="sm_90", ...)) rather than JIT-specialized the way Triton kernels are, which is what makes genuine, driver-free verification possible in a sandboxed environment at all.

The design principles carried through the whole book:

  • Kernels, not a framework. This book builds tile kernels against arrays and tensors that already exist — NumPy, CuPy, and PyTorch — the same choice the Triton edition makes and the CUDA/Mojo/Rust editions don't, because unlike those three, cuTile Python was never designed to own the tensor or the autograd graph.
  • Tiles and arrays are different types, on purpose. Every chapter is explicit about which operations a Tile supports that an Array does not, and why: it's the single largest conceptual difference from Triton's block-pointer model, and it's introduced in Part 0 before any kernel-writing begins.
  • Portability as a genuinely tested claim, not a slogan. The same kernel is ahead-of-time compiled in this book's own build environment to real cubin for multiple named target architectures (sm_80, sm_90, sm_100) with no GPU present at all — a form of real verification the CUDA book's plain nvcc compile doesn't have available to it, since cuTile Python's compiler resolves libcuda.so and any real device only at kernel-launch time, not at compile time.
  • Honest about verification on two different axes. Ahead-of-time compilation to a named architecture is genuinely run and its real output byte-counted. Anything that requires launching a kernel against a live CUDA stream and reading back a real numeric result is clearly tagged unverified until tested on real hardware — this book never presents a number it didn't actually measure, or blurs the line between what compiled and what ran.
  • Financial computing ready. The closing chapter validates these building blocks against the same kind of Black-Scholes, rolling-volatility, and Monte Carlo option-pricing problems the Mojo, Triton, CUDA, and Rust books end on.

  • :material-view-grid:{ .lg .middle } 21 chapters

    Part 0 through Part 7, from the tile/array distinction to a Monte Carlo option pricer.

  • :material-cube-scan:{ .lg .middle } Tiles vs. arrays

    Two distinct, statically-known types — immutable compute tiles and mutable strided global memory — genuinely distinguished throughout.

  • :material-chip:{ .lg .middle } Ahead-of-time, multi-target

    One kernel, genuinely compiled to real cubin for sm_80, sm_90, and sm_100 in this same sandboxed environment — no GPU required to prove it.

  • :material-finance:{ .lg .middle } Real financial models

    Black-Scholes, rolling volatility, and Monte Carlo pricing, cross-checked by a second independent method.

docs.title: How the book is organized
docs.text:
Part Focus Part 0 — cuTile Foundations Arrays, tiles, and the kernel boundary; kernel parameterization with ct.Constant; tiled views and memory layout; the cuTile programming model (grids, ct.bid); targeting hardware and ahead-of-time compilation Part 1 — Kernel–Array Interface The array–tile contract (ArrayConstraint, aliasing); divisibility and alignment hints; masking, padding, and rounding modes; the memory model (order, scope, atomics); autotuning with ct.tune Part 2 — Core Kernels Elementwise kernels, the tiled matmul kernel (ct.matmul, tensor cores), reduction and scan kernels Part 3 — Wiring Into PyTorch's Autograd torch.autograd.Function as the graph node Part 4 — The Backward Kernel Writing the backward kernel, chaining custom cuTile ops through autograd Part 5 — GPU Acceleration and Performance Compilation and export revisited (cubin vs. Tile IR bytecode, calling conventions), benchmarking honestly with no GPU present Part 6 — Neural Network Building Blocks Fused kernels for real layers, interoperability (SIMT interop, JAX FFI) and advanced fusion Part 7 — Financial Computing Applications Black-Scholes, rolling volatility, and Monte Carlo option pricing

Start with Getting Started to stand up a cuTile Python environment. Part 0 (cuTile Foundations) is next up and not yet written.

How this book relates to its siblings

Mojo, CUDA C++, and Rust all build their own tensor type and their own autodiff engine because none of them has anything else to lean on for this kind of from-scratch teaching arc. Triton deliberately does neither — it owns only the kernel and leans on PyTorch for the tensor, the device, and the autograd graph. cuTile Python follows Triton's arc, not Mojo/CUDA/Rust's: it has no built-in tensor abstraction and no autograd engine of its own, so this book doesn't build either — it builds kernels against PyTorch's, the same seam the Triton book uses. What's genuinely new here, with no equivalent in any of the four siblings, is the tile/array type split as a first-class language feature, and a compilation model where ahead-of-time export to a named target architecture is itself real, runnable, driver-free evidence — closer to what nvcc gives the CUDA book, but for a Python-hosted DSL. cuTile Python and Triton are also not unrelated projects sharing a family resemblance by accident: NVIDIA has built a Tile IR backend for Triton itself, so the same compiler infrastructure this book's kernels compile to is also, as of 2026, one of Triton's own compilation targets — a relationship this book's closing appendix examines directly, including the public disagreement between NVIDIA and Triton's original creators over it.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This book targets cuTile Python 1.5.0+ (the cuda-tile package on PyPI), running under Python 3.10 through 3.14. Every listing's definition and ahead-of-time compilation is genuinely run against the real package in this book's build environment. Actually launching a kernel needs a real NVIDIA GPU and driver, which this environment does not have — this book flags that explicitly wherever it applies (see How this book verifies its claims below).

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Install cuTile Python from PyPI. The [tileiras] extra bundles the ahead-of-time compiler as a set of pure-Python wheels, so it installs cleanly with no CUDA Toolkit and no NVIDIA driver present at all:

pip install "cuda-tile[tileiras]"

If you already have CUDA Toolkit 13.1+ installed system-wide, the compiler is picked up from there instead and the plain package is enough:

pip install cuda-tile

Confirm the install and check the version:

python3 -c "import cuda.tile as ct; print(ct.__version__)"

This book was written and verified against:

cuda-tile 1.5.0
Python 3.11.15

with pip install "cuda-tile[tileiras]" genuinely pulling in cuda-toolkit 13.3.1, nvidia-cuda-nvcc 13.3.73, nvidia-cuda-tileiras 13.3.36, nvidia-cuda-crt 13.3.73, nvidia-cuda-runtime 13.3.29, nvidia-nvvm 13.3.73, and nvidia-nvjitlink 13.3.33 — no driver, no GPU, and no separate system CUDA Toolkit install required for any of it.

The Python import path is not what the package name suggests

The PyPI package is cuda-tile, but the module it installs is cuda.tile, not cuda_tile. import cuda_tile as ct genuinely fails with ModuleNotFoundError in this environment; import cuda.tile as ct is the real, working import used throughout this book.

docs.title: Verify the toolchain — genuinely run, no GPU required
docs.text:
import cuda.tile as ct

@ct.kernel
def vector_add(a, b, c, tile_size: ct.Constant[int]):
    pid = ct.bid(0)
    a_tile = ct.load(a, index=(pid,), shape=(tile_size,))
    b_tile = ct.load(b, index=(pid,), shape=(tile_size,))
    result = a_tile + b_tile
    ct.store(c, index=(pid,), tile=result)

print(type(vector_add))

Genuinely run in this book's environment:

<class 'cuda.tile._execution.kernel'>

Defining a @ct.kernel function costs nothing GPU-related — it just builds a Python-level kernel object. If you see the same class name, your install is working and you're ready for ahead-of-time compilation, the next real step this book relies on.

docs.title: Ahead-of-time compilation — the part that works with no GPU at all
docs.text:
cuTile Python resolves the real GPU driver only when a kernel is launched, not when it's compiled for a named target architecture. That makes ct.compilation.export_kernel genuinely runnable in a driver-free sandbox — this book's equivalent of the CUDA edition's plain nvcc compile, but able to target multiple architectures from the same environment:

import io

sig = ct.compilation.KernelSignature(
    [
        ct.compilation.ArrayConstraint(
            ct.float32, ndim=1, index_dtype=ct.int32,
            stride_lower_bound_incl=0, alias_groups=[], may_alias_internally=False,
        ),
        ct.compilation.ArrayConstraint(
            ct.float32, ndim=1, index_dtype=ct.int32,
            stride_lower_bound_incl=0, alias_groups=[], may_alias_internally=False,
        ),
        ct.compilation.ArrayConstraint(
            ct.float32, ndim=1, index_dtype=ct.int32,
            stride_lower_bound_incl=0, alias_groups=[], may_alias_internally=False,
        ),
        ct.compilation.ConstantConstraint(256),
    ],
    calling_convention=ct.compilation.CallingConvention.cutile_python_v2(),
)

for arch in ("sm_80", "sm_90", "sm_100"):
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    ct.compilation.export_kernel(vector_add, [sig], buf, gpu_code=arch, output_format="cubin")
    print(arch, "cubin bytes:", len(buf.getvalue()))

Genuinely run in this book's environment:

sm_80 cubin bytes: 23728
sm_90 cubin bytes: 24736
sm_100 cubin bytes: 30760

Three real, differently-sized cubin binaries, one per target architecture, produced by the same Python function and the same tileiras compiler that ships with the [tileiras] extra — with no NVIDIA GPU, no driver, and no nvidia-smi anywhere in this environment. output_format="tileir_bytecode" genuinely works the same way if you want NVIDIA's intermediate representation instead of a finished binary.

docs.title: GPU toolchain (needed to actually launch a kernel)
docs.text:
Everything above — defining a kernel, building a KernelSignature, exporting real cubin or Tile IR bytecode for a named architecture — is genuine, driver-free evidence. Actually launching a kernel with ct.launch(stream, grid, kernel, kernel_args) needs a real CUDA stream, which in turn needs a real NVIDIA GPU, its driver, and typically a library like CuPy or PyTorch to construct that stream in the first place. This book's build environment has none of that, so no ct.launch() call anywhere in this book was actually attempted against a live device — that step is explicitly out of reach here, not attempted-and-hidden.

To run the kernels this book compiles, you'll need:

  • An NVIDIA GPU with compute capability 8.x, 9.x, 10.x, 11.x, or 12.x — as of the cuda-tile 1.5.0 README, the bundled tileiras compiler itself only targets Ampere/Ada and Blackwell GPUs; Hopper support is described there as coming in a future release, so check the installed nvidia-cuda-tileiras package's own notes if you're targeting Hopper specifically
  • NVIDIA Driver r580 or later
  • CuPy or PyTorch with CUDA support, to allocate real device arrays and obtain a real cudaStream_t-backed stream to pass to ct.launch
nvidia-smi      # confirms a real driver + GPU are present

A note on where this book's cuTile code was written

This book is authored and its ahead-of-time compilation steps are verified in a sandboxed environment with pip install "cuda-tile[tileiras]" genuinely succeeding and no NVIDIA GPU, driver, or nvidia-smi present at all. Every kernel definition and every ct.compilation.export_kernel call shown with real byte counts was genuinely run there. Any chapter or example that would require ct.launch against a live device is marked UNVERIFIED — pending a real-GPU test pass until independently run on real hardware and confirmed. If you're reading this after that pass, those tags should be gone and replaced with real captured output; if you still see one, that chapter hasn't been verified on hardware yet.

docs.title: How this book verifies its claims
docs.text: Every "Worked Example" in this book that defines a kernel or compiles it ahead-of-time embeds real, unedited output from the actual cuda-tile package run against the exact listing shown — nothing is hand-typed or guessed. Where a chapter makes a numeric or behavioral claim that only a real GPU could produce, it's explicitly tagged unverified rather than invented, exactly as described above, until run on real hardware and folded back in.
